lead: Leave an adsorbent in a fluid long enough and the loading stops changing: molecules land on the surface as fast as they leave it. The equilibrium loading q plotted against the fluid concentration C (or the partial pressure p of a gas) at one temperature is the adsorption isotherm. It tells the designer how much solute a kilogram of adsorbent can hold at the concentration it will see, and so how much adsorbent a duty needs. Two equations cover most exam questions: Langmuir and Freundlich.
prereq: You need the batch loading q = (C0 − Ce)V/W from Adsorption principles and adsorbents.

blocks.text: Flasks with the same volume V of solution but different starting concentrations C<sub>0</sub> (or different adsorbent masses W) are shaken at constant temperature until nothing changes. Each flask gives one pair: the equilibrium concentration C<sub>e</sub> left in the liquid and the loading q = (C<sub>0</sub> − C<sub>e</sub>)V/W. The isotherm is q against C<sub>e</sub>, the equilibrium concentration, never against the feed concentration. For a gas the same is done with the partial pressure p of the adsorbate.

At very low concentration most isotherms are straight, q = KC (Henry's law region). At higher concentration they bend. An isotherm that is concave towards the C axis, rising steeply and then levelling, is favourable: a lot is held even from a dilute fluid. A straight line is linear, and one that curves upward is unfavourable: little is held until the fluid is concentrated.

Langmuir assumed a surface of identical sites, each holding one molecule, with no forces between held molecules, so adsorption stops at a single complete layer. Equating the rate of landing on empty sites to the rate of leaving full ones gives:
q = q<sub>m</sub>K<sub>L</sub>C / (1 + K<sub>L</sub>C)      linear form: C/q = 1/(q<sub>m</sub>K<sub>L</sub>) + C/q<sub>m</sub>
blocks.where: q<sub>m</sub> is the monolayer capacity (mg/g); K<sub>L</sub> is the affinity constant (L/mg when C is in mg/L); C is the equilibrium concentration. A plot of C/q against C is a straight line of slope 1/q<sub>m</sub> and intercept 1/(q<sub>m</sub>K<sub>L</sub>), so q<sub>m</sub> = 1/slope and K<sub>L</sub> = slope/intercept. For a gas replace C by p and K<sub>L</sub> by b (1/bar).

blocks.text: At low C, K<sub>L</sub>C ≪ 1 and q ≈ q<sub>m</sub>K<sub>L</sub>C, the straight Henry's law region. At high C, K<sub>L</sub>C ≫ 1 and q approaches q<sub>m</sub>. A large K<sub>L</sub> means the solute is held strongly and the curve reaches its plateau at a low concentration. The dimensionless separation factor R<sub>L</sub> = 1/(1 + K<sub>L</sub>C<sub>0</sub>) sums up the shape: between 0 and 1 favourable, 1 linear, above 1 unfavourable.
Real surfaces have strong and weak sites. Freundlich's equation is empirical and fits such surfaces over a limited range:
q = K<sub>F</sub>C<sup>1/n</sup>      linear form: log q = log K<sub>F</sub> + (1/n) log C
blocks.where: K<sub>F</sub> is a capacity constant whose units, (mg/g)(L/mg)<sup>1/n</sup>, depend on n; 1/n (between 0 and 1 for a favourable isotherm) measures how quickly q levels off. A plot of log q against log C has slope 1/n and intercept log K<sub>F</sub>.

blocks.text: The Freundlich isotherm has no plateau: q keeps rising as C rises, so it must not be extrapolated far beyond the data it was fitted to. It is the usual form for activated carbon in water treatment, where concentrations are low.

Pressure. For a gas the loading depends on the partial pressure of the adsorbate, p = yP. Raising the total pressure at a fixed mole fraction raises p and so raises q; adding an inert gas does not. Pressure-swing adsorption loads a bed at high pressure and regenerates it by dropping to low pressure.

Temperature. Physical adsorption gives out heat, so at a fixed C or p a hotter adsorbent holds less. The constants qm, KL, KF and n belong to the temperature at which they were measured. Isotherms measured at two temperatures give the heat of adsorption from the pressures p1 and p2 needed for the same loading: ln(p2/p1) = (ΔHads/R)(1/T1 − 1/T2), with ΔHads taken as a positive heat released. Temperature-swing adsorption uses this: load cold, regenerate hot.
Other shapes exist. Where several layers build up, as in nitrogen on a solid near its boiling point, the BET isotherm is used, and its fit gives the surface area of an adsorbent.

examples.question: A dye on activated carbon at 25 °C follows the Langmuir isotherm with q<sub>m</sub> = 40 mg/g and K<sub>L</sub> = 1.5 L/mg. (a) Find q at C = 2.0 mg/L. (b) Find C when q = 20 mg/g. (c) Is the isotherm favourable for a feed of 10 mg/L?
steps: (b) 20 = 60C/(1 + 1.5C), so 20 + 30C = 60C and C = 20/30 = 0.667 mg/L. Half of q<sub>m</sub> is reached at C = 1/K<sub>L</sub>, which is the same 0.667 mg/L.
examples.answer: q = 30 mg/g at 2.0 mg/L; C = 0.667 mg/L at q = 20 mg/g; R<sub>L</sub> = 0.0625, favourable.

examples.question: Equilibrium tests for the same dye give: C (mg/L) 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0 and q (mg/g) 17.1, 24.0, 30.0, 35.3. Fit the Langmuir and the Freundlich equations by their linear plots and compare their predictions at C = 10 mg/L.
steps: Langmuir: C/q = 0.02924, 0.04167, 0.06667, 0.14164 g/L. A least-squares line through (C, C/q) has slope 0.02498 g/mg and intercept 0.01671 g/L.
q<sub>m</sub> = 1/0.02498 = 40.0 mg/g; K<sub>L</sub> = 0.02498/0.01671 = 1.50 L/mg. The points lie on the line, so Langmuir fits.

Freundlich: log C = −0.301, 0, 0.301, 0.699 and log q = 1.233, 1.380, 1.477, 1.548. The best line has slope 1/n = 0.311 (n = 3.22) and intercept 1.355, so K<sub>F</sub> = 10<sup>1.355</sup> = 22.7 (mg/g)(L/mg)<sup>0.311</sup>. The points bend away from this line at both ends.
At C = 10 mg/L: Langmuir q = 40 × 15/16 = 37.5 mg/g; Freundlich q = 22.7 × 10<sup>0.311</sup> = 46.3 mg/g.
Freundlich overshoots the monolayer capacity because it has no plateau; outside the measured range, trust the model whose straight-line plot actually fitted.
examples.answer: Langmuir: q<sub>m</sub> = 40.0 mg/g, K<sub>L</sub> = 1.50 L/mg. Freundlich: 1/n = 0.311, K<sub>F</sub> = 22.7. At 10 mg/L they predict 37.5 and 46.3 mg/g; the Langmuir value is the reliable one here.

traps: In the plot of C/q against C, the slope is 1/q<sub>m</sub> and the intercept is 1/(q<sub>m</sub>K<sub>L</sub>). Reading the intercept as q<sub>m</sub> is the commonest error.
In the Freundlich log plot, 1/n is the slope, not n. Invert the slope to get n.
Plot q against the equilibrium concentration C<sub>e</sub>, not against the starting concentration C<sub>0</sub>.
For a gas the loading follows the partial pressure of the adsorbate, not the total pressure.
An isotherm measured at 25 °C overestimates the loading of a bed run at 60 °C, since physical adsorption falls as temperature rises.

quiz.q: State the assumptions of the Langmuir isotherm.
quiz.a: Identical sites, one molecule per site, no interaction between held molecules, and adsorption limited to one layer; landing and leaving rates are equal at equilibrium.

quiz.q: Why does the Langmuir isotherm level off at high concentration while the Freundlich does not?
quiz.a: Langmuir has a finite number of sites, so q cannot exceed q<sub>m</sub> once the layer is full. Freundlich is an empirical power law, C<sup>1/n</sup>, which keeps rising without limit.

quiz.q: A carbon follows Langmuir with q<sub>m</sub> = 50 mg/g and K<sub>L</sub> = 0.8 L/mg. Find q at C = 5 mg/L.
Freundlich K<sub>F</sub> = 10 (mg/g)(L/mg)<sup>1/2</sup> and n = 2. Find q at 4 and at 8 mg/L.
quiz.a: q = 10 × 4<sup>0.5</sup> = 20 mg/g and 10 × 8<sup>0.5</sup> = 28.3 mg/g: doubling C raises q by √2.

quiz.q: A gas needs a partial pressure of 0.10 bar at 25 °C and 0.40 bar at 60 °C for the same loading. Estimate the heat of adsorption and say whether it is physical adsorption.
quiz.a: ΔH = R ln(p<sub>2</sub>/p<sub>1</sub>)/(1/T<sub>1</sub> − 1/T<sub>2</sub>) = 8.314 × ln 4/(1/298.15 − 1/333.15) = 11.53/3.523 × 10<sup>−4</sup> = 32.7 kJ/mol, in the physical adsorption range.

quiz.q: Carbon A has q<sub>m</sub> = 100 mg/g, K<sub>L</sub> = 0.1 L/mg; carbon B has q<sub>m</sub> = 40 mg/g, K<sub>L</sub> = 2 L/mg. Which is better at C = 0.1 mg/L and at C = 10 mg/L?
quiz.a: At 0.1 mg/L: A holds 100 × 0.01/1.01 = 0.99 mg/g, B holds 40 × 0.2/1.2 = 6.67 mg/g, so B wins on affinity. At 10 mg/L: A holds 100 × 1/2 = 50 mg/g, B holds 40 × 20/21 = 38.1 mg/g, so A wins on capacity. For polishing to low levels choose B.

beyond: Not for the exam. When several solutes compete for the same sites, as in real wastewater, the extended Langmuir and ideal adsorbed solution theory predict mixture loadings from single-solute isotherms. Gas adsorbers are designed from isotherms at several temperatures, and adsorption heat pumps and chillers run on the same data. Search for ideal adsorbed solution theory and BET isotherm.

figure.caption: Left: the four measured points (black), the Langmuir fit q = 40 × 1.5C/(1 + 1.5C) levelling at 40 mg/g, and the Freundlich fit, which has no plateau and overshoots at 10 mg/L (46.3 against 37.5 mg/g). The two large points are the first worked example. Right: the straight Langmuir plot of C/q against C that gives the constants.

spec.aria: Two graphs. Left, loading q against equilibrium concentration with four data points, a solid Langmuir curve approaching a dashed line at 40 mg/g and a dashed Freundlich curve that keeps rising. Right, C/q against C with the same four points on a straight line of slope 0.0250 and intercept 0.0167.
